title: Where does a stablecoin come from?
intro: Follow a digital dollar from its issuer to the exchanges and protocols that use it.

steps.text: Circle issues USDC. For every token it mints, it holds about a dollar in cash and short-term government debt. A company stands behind it, not a protocol.
USDC is minted natively on Ethereum and many other chains. On Ethereum it is an ERC-20 token: a smart contract that keeps a list of balances.
Exchanges are the on-ramp: you pay dollars and receive USDC, or the reverse. This is where most dollars enter and leave crypto.
On-chain, stablecoins sit in pools such as Curve's, so they can be swapped for each other cheaply, without an order book.
Not every on-chain dollar comes from a company. Sky (formerly MakerDAO) mints DAI and USDS against collateral that users lock in vaults.

title: How a swap on Base reaches Ethereum
intro: Follow one token swap from your wallet, through a Layer 2, down to Ethereum.

steps.text: You sign the swap in your wallet. The wallet never sends your private key, only a signed transaction.
The transaction runs on Base, a Layer 2. It is fast and cheap because it doesn't execute on Ethereum itself.
Uniswap's contracts on Base price the swap from the reserves in a pool: an automated market maker, with no order book.
Base posts batches of transactions to Ethereum and relies on it for security: wrong results can be caught and corrected there.
Base started on the OP Stack, a kit shared with OP Mainnet, Unichain and Ink. Many Layer 2s are built from the same parts.
Anyone can check the result on a block explorer: the transaction, the swap and the fee paid.

title: How Bitcoin scales
intro: Bitcoin stays simple on purpose. See what is built around it to do more.

steps.text: Bitcoin keeps its base layer simple and slow on purpose: about one block every ten minutes, with limited space in each.
Lightning moves payments into channels: two people lock bitcoin once, then exchange signed balance updates instantly, off-chain.
Stacks adds smart contracts and anchors its blocks to Bitcoin. Whether it counts as a true Layer 2 is debated.
Rootstock is an EVM-compatible sidechain. Bitcoin miners also mine its blocks, a technique called merged mining.

title: Where security and data come from
intro: Staked ETH secures Ethereum. See how the same stake is reused, and where rollups put their data.

steps.text: Validators stake ETH to secure Ethereum. If they misbehave, part of their stake can be taken away (slashed).
Lido turns staked ETH into a token, stETH, that keeps earning rewards and can be used elsewhere at the same time.
EigenLayer lets stakers restake ETH or stETH to secure other services, accepting extra slashing risk in exchange for extra rewards.
EigenDA is one of those services: it stores rollups' data more cheaply than Ethereum, backed by restaked ETH.
Celestia takes another route: a separate chain built only to publish and keep data available for rollups.
